title: How online orders find their way to your door: shipping and carrier management software
audience: A curious adult coming from a different field, with no assumed knowledge of logistics or e-commerce.
scope: Covers the software that sits between a shop's order systems and the companies that physically carry parcels and pallets: choosing delivery options at checkout, booking carriers, printing labels and documents, tracking, returns and checking transport costs. Examples come from the Netherlands and the wider European market, where DeliveryMatch operates. Warehousing (picking and packing), the carriers' own operations and customs law in detail are left out.
learningGoals: Explain why a shop that ships with several carriers needs a layer of software between its systems and the carriers.
Distinguish a delivery promise made at checkout from the delivery itself, and explain why stock and capacity matter for that promise.
Describe what happens between 'order placed' and 'parcel delivered', including documents and tracking.
Explain how shippers, carriers, fulfilment companies and software partners each gain from such a platform, and where their interests conflict.
Recognise the main hard problems: keeping promises, controlling cost, handling exceptions and returns, and integrating many systems.

introduction.whatItIs: When you buy something online, the shop has to decide how your order travels: which delivery company (a 'carrier'), which service (next day, evening, pickup point), from which warehouse, at what cost. Then someone must tell the carrier the parcel is coming, print a label, and keep you informed. Shipping and carrier management software does this work for many orders at once, connecting the shop's systems with dozens or hundreds of carriers.
introduction.whyItMatters: Delivery is the part of online shopping the customer physically experiences. A wrong promise, a lost parcel or a painful return costs the shop the next sale, while transport is one of its largest costs. For businesses shipping thousands of parcels a day, doing this by hand in carrier websites is slow, error-prone and impossible to control.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of a travel booking site for parcels. A traveller compares airlines on price, time and comfort, books one, gets a boarding pass and receives updates. The shipping platform compares carriers, books one, prints the 'boarding pass' (the label) and sends updates.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Unlike a traveller, a parcel cannot choose for itself, and the 'booking' often has to happen before anyone knows exactly when the goods will be ready. The shop also promises a delivery date to its customer before the carrier has even been chosen, so the software must reason about stock, warehouse deadlines and carrier capacity at the moment of purchase.

participants.name: The shopper or recipient
participants.role: Chooses a delivery option, receives the parcel and sometimes returns it.
participants.caresAbout: Knowing when it arrives, choosing where, paying little, and returning easily.

participants.name: The shipper (webshop, retailer, wholesaler or manufacturer)
participants.role: Sells the goods, makes the delivery promise and pays for transport; buys the shipping software.
participants.caresAbout: Keeping promises at the lowest sensible cost without extra staff.

participants.name: The fulfilment company (3PL)
participants.role: Stores and ships goods on behalf of many shops.
participants.caresAbout: Throughput, getting new client shops live quickly, and earning a margin on shipping.

participants.name: The carrier or broker
participants.role: Physically moves parcels or pallets; a broker resells capacity from several carriers.
participants.caresAbout: Receiving clean, pre-announced shipments and being paid correctly.

participants.name: The software partner
participants.role: Makes the shop's webshop, ERP (business administration) or warehouse system and connects it to the shipping platform.
participants.caresAbout: Offering shipping features without building carrier links themselves.

participants.name: The shipping platform provider (for example DeliveryMatch)
participants.role: Operates the software in the middle and maintains connections to carriers and systems.
participants.caresAbout: Reliable connections, happy shippers, and growth in the volume flowing through.

concepts.meaning: Using several carriers through one system, choosing per shipment.
concepts.example: A shop sends small parcels with one carrier, heavy items with another, and pallets with a freight company - all from the same screen.
concepts.whyItMatters: No single carrier is best for everything; choice lowers cost and risk, but only if switching is easy.

media.alt: Multi-carrier shipping: A shop sends small parcels with one carrier, heavy items with another, and pallets with a freight company - all from the same screen.
media.caption: No single carrier is best for everything; choice lowers cost and risk, but only if switching is easy.

concepts.meaning: Telling the carrier in advance about a shipment and receiving a tracking number and a barcode label to stick on it.
concepts.example: The warehouse scans an order; the system sends the data to the carrier and prints the label within seconds.
concepts.whyItMatters: A parcel without correct pre-announcement may be refused or delayed at the depot.

media.title: Pre-announcement and label
media.alt: Pre-announcement and label: The warehouse scans an order; the system sends the data to the carrier and prints the label within seconds.
media.caption: A parcel without correct pre-announcement may be refused or delayed at the depot.

concepts.meaning: What the shop tells the customer about when and how the parcel will arrive, made at checkout.
concepts.example: 'Delivered Thursday between 18:00 and 21:00' or 'Pick up from Friday at the corner shop'.
concepts.whyItMatters: The promise is made before the parcel exists; if stock or capacity are wrong, the shop breaks its word.

media.title: Delivery promise
media.alt: Delivery promise: 'Delivered Thursday between 18:00 and 21:00' or 'Pick up from Friday at the corner shop'.
media.caption: The promise is made before the parcel exists; if stock or capacity are wrong, the shop breaks its word.

concepts.meaning: A checkout that calculates delivery options live from stock, address, carrier services and capacity instead of showing fixed choices.
concepts.example: If one item comes from a supplier next week, the checkout only offers dates from next week, or a split delivery.
concepts.whyItMatters: It turns logistics from reacting after the order ('push') into steering at the moment of purchase ('pull').

media.title: Dynamic checkout
media.alt: Dynamic checkout: If one item comes from a supplier next week, the checkout only offers dates from next week, or a split delivery.
media.caption: It turns logistics from reacting after the order ('push') into steering at the moment of purchase ('pull').

concepts.meaning: If-then logic that decides carrier, service and price per order.
concepts.example: 'Orders above 30 kg to Germany go by pallet carrier X; orders from the marketplace use service Y.'
concepts.whyItMatters: Rules capture the shop's strategy and customer agreements so staff do not have to remember them.

media.title: Shipping rules
media.alt: Shipping rules: 'Orders above 30 kg to Germany go by pallet carrier X; orders from the marketplace use service Y.'
media.caption: Rules capture the shop's strategy and customer agreements so staff do not have to remember them.

concepts.meaning: Papers or data that let goods travel legally: consignment notes (CMR) for road freight, customs invoices for export, dangerous-goods (ADR) declarations.
concepts.example: A battery shipment to Switzerland needs both a customs invoice and dangerous-goods labels.
concepts.whyItMatters: Missing documents stop shipments at borders or depots.

media.title: Transport documents
media.alt: Transport documents: A battery shipment to Switzerland needs both a customs invoice and dangerous-goods labels.
media.caption: Missing documents stop shipments at borders or depots.

concepts.meaning: Status messages from the carrier: collected, sorted, out for delivery, delivered, failed.
concepts.example: 'Delivery attempt failed - recipient not home' arrives at 14:02.
concepts.whyItMatters: They drive customer messages and let the shop act before the customer complains.

media.title: Tracking events
media.alt: Tracking events: 'Delivery attempt failed - recipient not home' arrives at 14:02.
media.caption: They drive customer messages and let the shop act before the customer complains.

concepts.meaning: Comparing what the carrier invoices with what the shipment should have cost.
concepts.example: The invoice adds a size surcharge on a parcel that was booked as standard size.
concepts.whyItMatters: Small overcharges across thousands of parcels add up; without expected costs there is nothing to compare.

media.alt: Freight audit (carrier invoice control): The invoice adds a size surcharge on a parcel that was booked as standard size.
media.caption: Small overcharges across thousands of parcels add up; without expected costs there is nothing to compare.

history.change: Shops booked shipments in each carrier's own website or software and printed labels per carrier.
history.whyItMatters: Every new carrier meant a new screen and a new process, which kept most shops on one carrier.

history.change: E-commerce growth brought independent multi-carrier platforms; in the Netherlands, research into consumers' delivery wishes (by DeliveryMatch's founder from 2009 to 2012) led to the idea that delivery choice belongs in the checkout. DeliveryMatch was founded in 2013 and its first customer went live in 2014.
history.whyItMatters: Delivery became a sales feature, not just a cost.

history.change: Platforms connected to hundreds of carriers and business systems; pickup points, lockers and evening delivery spread across Europe.
history.whyItMatters: Choice exploded, so deciding automatically between options became the main value.

history.change: Consolidation: larger groups formed (for example nShift in 2021 from several Nordic and Dutch vendors) and software groups such as Katapull combined complementary products - ERP, point of sale, marketplaces, EDI, returns, warehouse and shipping.
history.whyItMatters: Shipping software increasingly competes as part of an ecosystem rather than as a standalone tool.

historyNote: This is a selective, mostly Dutch and European view; other markets developed differently.

walkthrough.title: One order for a camera bag and a tripod (illustrative example)
walkthrough.setup: Fictional characters: Sanne runs operations at a mid-size Dutch photography webshop that sells through its own site and a marketplace. The bag is in the shop's warehouse; the tripod is held by a supplier that ships directly. A shopper, Jeroen, orders both on a Tuesday evening.

steps.title: Jeroen sees delivery options
steps.whatHappens: At checkout the platform checks stock: the bag is available now, the tripod ships from the supplier tomorrow. It offers Thursday home delivery for both parcels or a pickup point, with prices and an estimated CO2 figure.
steps.whyItMatters: The promise is based on real stock and carrier services, so it can be kept.
steps.watchOut: If the supplier's stock feed is out of date, the promise is wrong from the start.

steps.title: The order arrives in the shipping platform
steps.whatHappens: The webshop passes the order to the platform; Jeroen's address is checked and rules choose carriers for the warehouse parcel and the supplier parcel.
steps.whyItMatters: No one re-types the order or decides manually.

steps.title: The warehouse scans and ships
steps.whatHappens: Next morning a packer scans the bag's order; the platform pre-announces it to the carrier, prints the label and sends Jeroen a branded message. The supplier books its parcel through the same platform.
steps.whyItMatters: One scan replaces several manual steps; both parcels are visible in one place.

steps.title: A delay appears
steps.whatHappens: On Wednesday night the tripod parcel misses a sorting connection. The tracking event triggers an alert in Sanne's exception list and a message to Jeroen with the new day.
steps.whyItMatters: The shop informs the customer before he asks.
steps.watchOut: Different carriers describe the same problem with different codes; the platform has to translate them.

steps.title: Jeroen returns the bag
steps.whatHappens: The bag is the wrong size. Jeroen registers a return in the shop's portal, chooses a drop-off point and prints a return label.
steps.whyItMatters: An easy return keeps him as a customer; the reason code tells the shop something about its size descriptions.

steps.title: The invoice is checked
steps.whatHappens: At month end the carrier's invoice is compared with the expected cost stored at booking; an unexpected surcharge is flagged for dispute.
steps.whyItMatters: The shop pays what it agreed, not what was billed by mistake.

walkthrough.outcome: Jeroen received his order as promised (one parcel a day late, but announced), returned an item without effort, and will probably order again. Sanne's team touched the order only to handle the exception, and the shop knows what the delivery really cost.

valueAndIncentives.title: Shippers save labour and keep promises
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Automation removes manual bookings and errors; reliable promises raise conversion and repeat purchases. Shippers pay a subscription and often usage-based fees (pricing is not published by DeliveryMatch).
valueAndIncentives.example: A shop that books thousands of parcels a week no longer needs staff copying addresses into carrier websites.

valueAndIncentives.title: Carriers want volume, shippers want freedom
valueAndIncentives.explanation: A platform makes it easy to add a carrier - and just as easy to move volume away. Carriers gain reach but lose some lock-in.
valueAndIncentives.example: A rule change can move all heavy parcels from one carrier to another overnight.

valueAndIncentives.title: 3PLs earn a margin on shipping
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Fulfilment companies buy transport at their rates and re-sell it to client shops; software that calculates sales rates and audits invoices protects that margin.
valueAndIncentives.example: A 3PL charges a client EUR 5.50 per parcel while paying the carrier less; freight audit catches surcharges that would erase the difference (illustrative figures).

valueAndIncentives.title: Software partners and groups gain features
valueAndIncentives.explanation: ERP, warehouse and webshop vendors embed shipping instead of building carrier links; in a group like Katapull, connected products make the whole offer stickier.
valueAndIncentives.example: A warehouse system sends shipment requests to the shipping platform and receives labels back.

challenges.title: Promising what can be delivered
challenges.whyHard: The promise is made before goods are picked, using stock data from other systems and carrier capacity that changes daily.
challenges.tradeOff: Fast promises sell better; safe promises are kept more often.
challenges.example: A checkout shows next-day delivery for an item that is actually at a supplier.
challenges.commonApproach: Stock-aware promise calculation and cut-off rules; it is only as good as the stock data it receives.

challenges.title: Keeping hundreds of connections alive
challenges.whyHard: Every carrier, webshop, ERP and marketplace has its own interface, and they change.
challenges.tradeOff: More connections attract customers but cost constant maintenance.
challenges.example: A carrier changes its label format and labels are rejected at the depot.
challenges.commonApproach: A uniform internal model with adapters per carrier and system; still needs a dedicated team.

challenges.title: Controlling transport cost
challenges.whyHard: Tariffs, zones, fuel and size surcharges differ by carrier and change often; invoices arrive weeks later.
challenges.tradeOff: Detailed cost models take effort to maintain; simple ones miss surcharges.
challenges.example: Oversize surcharges on 2% of parcels double the expected monthly cost increase.
challenges.commonApproach: Calculate expected cost at booking and audit invoices automatically; depends on accurate rate cards.

challenges.title: Exceptions and returns
challenges.whyHard: Delays, failed deliveries and returns are irregular and involve several parties.
challenges.tradeOff: Generous returns win customers but cost money.
challenges.example: A parcel shows 'delivered' but the customer has not received it.
challenges.commonApproach: Normalised tracking, alerts and self-service returns portals with rules for return costs.

misconceptions.reality: Label printing is the visible part; the value lies in deciding the carrier, making a keepable promise, informing the customer and controlling cost.

misconceptions.belief: Faster delivery is always what customers want.
misconceptions.reality: Many consumers prefer certainty and choice over speed; DeliveryMatch cites research that most will wait several days if the delivery moment is clear.

misconceptions.belief: Using more carriers always makes things more complicated.
misconceptions.reality: With a platform in the middle, more carriers mainly add choice; the complexity sits in the platform's connections and rules.

takeaways: Shipping software sits between order systems and carriers and turns each order into a booked, labelled, tracked shipment.
The delivery promise is made at checkout, before the parcel exists, so it depends on stock and capacity data.
Rules and automatic selection replace human decisions per order; exceptions are where people still add value.
Cost control requires knowing the expected cost of each shipment before the invoice arrives.
Value grows with connections - to carriers, business systems and partner products - which is why ecosystems like Katapull matter.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why might a checkout show a later delivery date for an order with two items than for each item separately?
knowledgeChecks.answer: Because one item is not in stock or ships from another location, so the complete order can only be delivered later.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A stock-aware promise looks at when the whole order can be delivered, unless split delivery is allowed.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a shop need in order to check a carrier invoice automatically?
knowledgeChecks.answer: The expected cost of each shipment calculated at booking from the agreed rates.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Without an expected cost per shipment there is nothing to compare the invoice line with.

knowledgeChecks.question: In the walkthrough, how did the shop learn about the tripod delay before Jeroen asked?
knowledgeChecks.answer: A tracking event from the carrier triggered an exception alert and a message.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Normalised tracking events let the platform spot deviations from expected milestones.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why could a carrier be both happy and worried about shippers using a multi-carrier platform?
knowledgeChecks.answer: It gains access to many shippers but can lose volume quickly when a rule changes.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The platform lowers switching costs in both directions.
